excerpt: Microsoft Authenticator is a free app that helps you sign in to all your accounts without using a password - just use a fingerprint, face recognition, or a PIN.
The codes don't require you to be on the internet or connected to data, so you don't need phone service to sign in.
You can set up notifications for your work or school account (if allowed by your administrator) or for your personal Microsoft account.
Verified IDs are secure trusted credentials that can be used by websites and organizations to make account setup simpler and safer.

When App Lock is enabled, you'll be asked to authenticate using your device PIN or biometric every time you open Authenticator.
To see your OTP codes in screenshots or allow other apps to capture the Authenticator screen, turn on Screen Capture in Authenticator's Settings and restart the app.
Scan the QR code or download and install Authenticator from the Apple app store.

This article describes how to back up information on all the accounts you have in Authenticator so that if you lose your mobile or get a new device, you can sign in to restore previously saved accounts
Scroll down to the Autofill section and select Export Passwords.
As the only way to sign in - just tap an approval on your phone to sign in. This is called going passwordless.
As a way to sign in every time, by using a one-time password code to increase account security. This is called two-step verification or multi-factor authentication.
Turn on the Cloud Backup toggle. Select a Microsoft personal account where the backup will be stored.
Scroll down to the Autofill section and select Export Passwords... Import your passwords.

To back up your Authenticator one-time password codes and account names on an iOS device, enable iCloud Drive, iCloud Keychain, and iCloud Backup for Authenticator.

This happened to me when I updated MS Authenticator after not updating it for a while. It wiped out all data, and I got locked out of all accounts. MS Authenticator is not a carefully written product.
I've been using Microsoft's one for my work accounts... I've never gotten that dialog, and have not had any issues with the accounts I've added.

using microsoft authenticator I just ran into this recently... it's a known issue that microsoft has no announced plan of fixing... I knew to cancel the dialogue and manually add the account without the QR code to workaround it.
Even for Microsoft accounts, use an alternative app for 2FA/MFA. Recently I switched to the open source Aegis, which allows encrypted backups and does not have the issue described.
It also tracks your position all the time. That is the bigger problem to me. [exodus-privacy report on com.azure.authenticator]

people pick MS Authenticator - it's because microsoft basically forces it on you, uses dark patterns to avoid letting you use any other standard OTP app and doesn't give admins the tools to disable it... The QR code they get is not a standard TOTP one, so any other client will reject it.
I have many accounts with the same user names, and they don't get overwritten. There might be some design flaw somewhere, but it's surely not what the article states.
IME some MS shops enforce use of it for 2fa to access company resources like vpn and etc. - for eg, the only reason this app exists on my phone is so I can log into my employer's vpn.

My company used to allow TOTP so many TOTP apps could be used instead of Microsoft Authenticator but my company disabled that a while ago. Now the only authenticator app my company allows is Microsoft Authenticator using push notifications.
it seems to be a push notification where the ms authenticator doesn't generate a code until I first log into the vpn using exchange creds.
Microsoft Authenticator--a mobile app that provides 2FA--is discontinuing its password autofill feature and the passwords stored/used with that will be wiped in August unless action is taken.
A user said updating Microsoft Authenticator after a long gap wiped all its data and locked them out of all their accounts, calling it 'not a carefully written product.'
A user uses Microsoft Authenticator for work accounts that nearly all share the same work email as the account name. They have never seen the overwrite dialog or had problems with any added accounts.

A user tested adding multiple accounts with the same email and found no conflict; each entry kept its issuer and matching icon. They have used MS Authenticator for years with the same username everywhere and never had the overwrite problem.

A user recently hit the account-overwrite issue and found it was a known problem with no announced fix. Their workaround: cancel the dialog and add the account manually instead of scanning the QR code.
A user recommends using a different app even for Microsoft accounts. They switched to the open-source Aegis, which supports encrypted backups and does not have the overwrite issue.
A user complained that the app tracks your position all the time and cited an Exodus Privacy report on com.azure.authenticator as their bigger concern.

An admin said Microsoft forces MS Authenticator on users: it cannot be disabled while other methods can, and the TOTP option is labeled 'Microsoft Authenticator.' The QR code shown is non-standard and other apps reject it; only a small 'use another app' link gives a real TOTP code.
Workaround: before adding a TOTP account to the authenticator app, scan the QR code with a QR reader and save the secret in a password manager as a backup.

An iOS user said the app shows a notice that Autofill via Authenticator ends in July 2025, with password export available until then. The iOS autofill provider moves to Edge, which still fills passwords in any app or browser through the native mechanism.

A user said the iOS app guided them to switch the system password manager setting to Edge. Since they already use Edge, it was a minor inconvenience, and Safari autofill from Edge works seamlessly. They found it odd that Edge must now be installed for the same functionality.

A user said the Microsoft Authenticator iOS app is probably the worst-designed app from a large corporation, where nothing works as expected. In one case a modal covered the 2FA code, offering only an option to hide the modal for 10 seconds to read the number.
A user complained that backing up Authenticator data to iCloud requires a personal Microsoft account and does not honor their paid business subscription.
A user said that despite careful privacy settings, their passwords somehow ended up in the Microsoft Authenticator app across several phone upgrades.

A user objected to the app deleting stored passwords: 'You can stop supporting new ones, but as soon as you destroy old ones YOU are a vulnerability... How can I ever trust you to not delete secrets in future?'
An IT person said small-business staff are mandated to run MS Authenticator for O365 on personal devices. They are trialing WinAuth on Windows desktops for remote users and are happy with it so far.
A user objected that employers' IT departments expect them to install MS Authenticator on their personal smartphone just to authenticate to Microsoft for the organization.
A user complained that Microsoft tries to force its own app instead of other 2FA providers and steers users heavily toward installing Microsoft apps.

A user with a stock, unrooted, up-to-date phone said Microsoft randomly flags it as 'rooted' and blocks access until a reboot, a few times a month. They worry about false positives now that credentials will be wiped.

A GrapheneOS user was disappointed the OS is treated as rooted despite being more secure than stock Android, and worried about being locked out of their 365 admin account. Disabling the hardened memory allocator may delay detection.
A user said actively wiping account data on phones detected as rooted is a reason never to use MS Authenticator for anything important, and is reconsidering their 2FA providers.
